2	title: "nagara: docs"
3	summary: "The docs: what each folder holds, how files are named, and how to write a note."
4	---
5	
6	# nagara: docs
7	
8	## What each folder holds
9	
10	| Folder | Holds | Index |
11	|---|---|---|
12	| `technical-design/` | How the code works: the item lifecycle, article extraction, read-along timing, the TTS service, the item contract, persistence and storage, authentication, deployment and CI, the invariants | [Technical design](technical-design/README.md) |
13	| `product-design/` | What nagara is: the ながら聞き premise, the listening experience, what gets read aloud, the queue | [Product design](product-design/README.md) |
14	
15	Which folder a note belongs in is a question about its subject, not about who wrote it. Code reading as a short placeholder rather than being read aloud is product design: it is a statement about what a listener experiences. The markdown-it-py token walk that produces that placeholder is technical design. The 100 ms inter-paragraph pause is product design, a number about how listening feels; folding it into the preceding timing window so there is no dead highlight zone is technical design. A note that needs both goes wherever it is mostly about and links across.
16	
17	`_templates/` holds no notes. The underscore is a sorting convention and nothing more: it floats the folder to the top of the file explorer.
18	
19	Work in flight lives in Linear, not here. A note describes something that exists; the issue that asked for it, and the open questions around it, live on the nagara project there. A note never links to an issue: the issue closes and the link rots, while the note is maintained for as long as the part exists.
20	
21	## Naming
22	
23	A note is named after the aspect it explains, in kebab-case. Not after its folder, not numbered, not dated: a date is a frontmatter field, so an index can sort on it without every filename carrying one.
24	
25	File names are unique across the whole docs folder, so a link never has to be disambiguated. Before adding a note, check the name is not taken.
26	
27	Every folder's index is called `README.md`, so that name is the one deliberate collision here: the payoff is that each index renders as a folder front page when the repository is browsed on the web. A link to a folder's index names the folder: `[the technical design](technical-design/README.md)`.
28	
29	## Frontmatter
30	
31	Every note carries `title` and `summary`, plus `created`. The summary is what shows up in search, in hover previews and in the indexes, so write it as a sentence about the subject rather than about the note.
32	
33	## How to write a note
34	
35	**A note explains how one part works.** It opens with an overview a reader can stop after, then the mechanism: the shape of the data, what calls what, in what order, with a diagram when the subject is a flow, a tree or a sequence. A reader should be able to hold that part of the system in their head without opening `api/app` or `tts/app.py` first.
36	
37	`_templates/note.md` offers the sections a note can use. They are a menu, not a required shape and not a closed list: keep the ones the subject needs, add one the menu lacks when the subject asks for it, and order them so the note is easiest to follow rather than in the order the template lists them. Edge cases and failure modes go in the prose or in a callout, never in a section of their own.
38	
39	**Reasoning goes in a callout, beside the thing it justifies**, not as the spine of the note:
40	
41	```markdown
42	> [!NOTE] Why no headless browser
43	> A plain fetch handled every HTML fixture tried, including a JS-rendered Substack post: it server-renders its content. The boundary sits further out than assumed.
44	```
45	
46	A note that opens with the argument for a design makes the reader meet the case for the architecture before the architecture itself, and the argument is not what they came for. It is still worth keeping (it is what lets a decision be revisited rather than re-argued); it just is not the spine. Per-decision *why* is also the one thing the code already has, densely, at the point of each decision; what code cannot give anyone is the shape of the whole.
47	
48	Three callout kinds, and they mean different things:
49	
50	- `> [!NOTE]`: a real choice, and why it went that way.
51	- `> [!WARNING]`: a failure mode: what breaks, how it presents, and whether anything catches it. Prefer failures that have actually happened.
52	- `> [!TIP]`: an alternative considered and not taken, with the reason it was not.
53	
54	**A note is not a decision record.** There is no requirements table, no acceptance criteria, no user story, no status ladder. Those describe work being planned; a note describes something that exists.
55	
56	**A note describes the present.** No "used to", no "previously", no "no longer". An alternative that was rejected is *considered and not chosen, because…*, a standing reason, not a history of the argument.
57	
58	Create a note from `_templates/note.md`. Then **link it from at least one existing note** and add its row to its folder's index: a note nothing links to does not get read.
59	
60	## House style
61	
62	- **No hard wrapping.** One line per paragraph; let the editor wrap. Diffs then show changed sentences rather than reflowed blocks.
63	- **Explain the code, do not reprint it.** A note is not a second copy of a declaration. What each member answers goes in a table, behaviour goes in a diagram or in prose, and a snippet appears only where the code itself is the insight: an exact formula, a guard whose precise form is the point. Two to four lines when it happens. Written the other way, a note comes out a third fenced code, in a second place where nothing typechecks it and it quietly falls out of date.
64	- **Mermaid, not ASCII**, for anything with a shape. A state machine, a data model, a request's path through the system and a tree all read faster as a diagram than as a paragraph describing one, and both GitHub and Obsidian render mermaid.
65	- **Headings name their subject, and carry an emoji.** "Extraction" and "The extraction" give a reader nothing to search for; "how a URL becomes paragraphs" does. Prefer a heading that could answer a question someone typed into search. Every heading in a note opens with one emoji chosen for its subject (`## 💽 Modeling`, `### 🔑 Login`), so a reader scanning the outline sees the shape of the note before the words; the template carries the usual ones and a section you add picks its own.
66	- **Say what a thing is.** Staging a sentence against its own opposite ("it does not reject the unknown kind, it ignores it") reads as emphasis while carrying no information the plain form lacks. Write the plain form.
67	- **Prefer commas, colons and full stops to dashes.** A paragraph leaning on dashes is usually one that wants to be two sentences.
68	- **Write about our implementation.** A comparison with some other tool belongs inside a callout that justifies a decision, and nowhere else; a note is not a literature review.
69	- Close a note with a `---` rule and a `Related:` line linking the notes it actually touches.
70	
71	## Adding a folder
72	
73	A folder is three things, and they have to agree:
74	
75	1. The directory.
76	2. A `README.md` in it, carrying that folder's index.
77	3. A row in the folder table above.
78	
79	`mahou:init` will do all three and leave anything that already exists alone, or do it by hand from this list: the skills read what is here either way. What breaks is doing two of the three: a folder with no row is invisible to anyone reading this file, and a row with no folder sends people looking for something that is not there.
80

1	# Markdown and lists: settled design
2	
3	## 1 What a unit's display markdown carries
4	- Unit kinds stay paragraph / code / image; a paragraph unit's display is GFM.
5	- Headings are paragraph units carrying `#`, quotes carry `>`; a list or table inside a quote stays in the quote's unit.
6	- Tables are GFM pipe tables; strikethrough is `~~`; task lists keep `[x]` / `[ ]`.
7	- A formula is its alttext as plain text, no delimiter.
8	- Attributions (blockquote footer/cite), `<dl>`, footnotes (refs and list) and self-links in headings are left out of the units.
9	- Inline elements with no GFM form keep whatever Turndown outputs.
10	- A list is one unit; nested lists stay inside their outer list's unit; ordered lists keep their numbers, including `start`.
11	- A list splits around every code block (`<pre>` / `<pre><code>`) or image inside it, at any depth, so the describer describes it; the part after continues the numbering and opens with an empty item at each enclosing level (compact CommonMark form `2.  3.  Item`), so resumed items keep their depth. Inline code stays inside the item.
12	- The title is the first unit, `# <title>`, built from extraction.title; no other unit carries the title.
13	- Not considered: image in a table cell, a table cell holding a list or code.
14	
15	## 2 How an element becomes markdown
16	- One shared converter for every recipe; a recipe never converts by hand.
17	- toMarkdown serializes the element including its own tag (today it uses cheerio `.html()`, the inner HTML, which drops the tag: the cause of 0/53 headings with `#`, 0/16 quotes with `>`, ordered lists as `-` in production).
18	- A `<pre>` without a `<code>` child gets its content wrapped in `<code>` before conversion, so every `<pre>` becomes a fenced block.
19	- Turndown with the fixed config (ATX, fenced, `-`, `---`) plus the GFM plugin.
20	- The validator checks the units the recipe declared (real element paths, checks unchanged). After a clean validation, the runtime splits list units holding a code block or an image into list part / code or image unit / list part, converts each part with the same converter, prepends the title unit, and returns the flattened list: what crosses to the API and what the agent's extract tool shows.
21	- Not considered: telling code `<pre>` from non-code, empty markdown for a declared element, a table with no header row, Turndown's escaping.
22	
23	## 3 What a recipe must do
24	- Prompt: markdown is GFM, hand toMarkdown the whole element; a list is one unit, never one per `<li>`, even with code or images; the runtime may split a unit into several and the extract tool shows the split result; formulas as plain alttext, no delimiter; leave out attributions, `<dl>`, footnotes, heading self-links and any heading repeating the title, through the recipe's own includes/ignores (leftover check unchanged); keep task-list checkboxes.
25	- The author and revision prompts carry the same rules.
26	- Validator: an `<li>` without a wrapping `<ol>`/`<ul>` is a problem, sent back for revision; no other prompt rule is checked; no check that headings/quotes/lists kept their markdown.
27	- Not considered: an agent failing a rule after its revisions run out.
28	
29	## 4 How the spoken form is derived from the display
30	- Derived from display by walking its markdown token tree.
31	- Headings, quotes and the title unit are read as their words, markers dropped.
32	- Every block inside a unit is on its own line (newline); nothing runs together (today paragraphs and list items fuse: `'First itemSecond item'`).
33	- A list item is its own line, no full stop added; ordered items keep `1.` at the start of the line; nesting depth is not announced.
34	- A split list's empty item has no spoken line.
35	- Task checkboxes are stripped; struck-through text is read as its words with no sign.
36	- A table's header row is spoken on its own line, then each body row as "Header: cell, …" on its own line.
37	- Code and image units keep their current spoken forms and the describer.
38	- Sanitize tail: keeps stripping leftover emphasis/code markers (still needed for run-in emphasis from Turndown); an asterisk only when it touches text; keeps newlines; only a `<word>` pair reduces to its word; then operator sequences become words, longest match first: `<=` less than or equal to, `>=` greater than or equal to, `->` to, `=>` to, `<-` from, `<<` much less than, `>>` much greater than, `<3` heart, `<` less than, `>` greater than. The describer's output runs through the same tail.
39	- Not considered: formula LaTeX read character by character, a line inside a unit with nothing to pronounce.
40	
41	## 5 How line structure reaches the audio
42	- One spoken string per unit, lines separated by newlines; the synthesizer's input shape is unchanged; tts/ does not change.

The domain-queue creates the instance before it persists the lease, both inside its single-threaded window, so a failed create leaves no lease behind. 134 135 ## 🧭 The job index 136 137 A singleton index Durable Object maps job id to domain in a SQLite table. Each domain-queue writes its entry while enqueuing, so the write happens inside the queue's own step instead of a second moving piece in the route. The read asks the Workflows API first, which answers any id that has an instance; when the id does not resolve because the job is still waiting in a FIFO, the entrypoint reads the domain from the index and that job's domain-queue answers the state. Entries are write-once: the index's alarm sweeps entries past a cutoff, and nothing deletes on the read or create path. 138 139 ## 🧩 The recipe runtime 140 141 | Member | Answers | Who asks | 142 |---|---|---| 143 | `run(recipe source, html)` | the title and the units, or the validation report | the workflow's run step, and the agents' one tool | 144 | `validate(extraction, html)` | the mechanical checks' report alone, over the recipe's units, container, inventory and ignores | `run`, on every execution | 145 146 `run` executes the script inside a Dynamic Worker: the injection bundle carries cheerio, domino, and turndown with it, the article parses inside because the recipe's `$` must exist there, and what returns is JSON. The validator is not part of the bundle; the mechanical checks run in the main Worker, so one implementation serves the workflow path and the agent tool path. A recipe that does not parse, throws against changed markup, or hangs until the CPU cap kills it, is a validation failure: the revision path's trigger, with its crash report as the validator report. A module that does not parse never starts the Dynamic Worker, so it cannot report itself as data; the load failure is recognised from the platform's own error, which names `recipe.js` in some runtimes and raises a bare `SyntaxError` in others. Only platform failures outside the recipe are `error` terminals: a Dynamic Worker that is unreachable, a bundle that does not load. 147 148 ## 🤖 The agents 149 150 Each dispatch opens a conversation keyed by the job id. The conversation is disposable, carries no history from other jobs, and its prompts are self-contained. A retry of the whole run is a fresh conversation under a suffixed id. The bounds are one hundred turns, authoring one retry, revision two, set in configuration with the model; the model is flash-class, to be chosen by evaluation before the agent round runs. The settled reply is a script validated in-loop by its own tool calls, a not-article verdict from the author, or the agent giving up. The reply never carries units. The workflow runs every settled script through the runtime, so a fresh recipe and a years-old one extract through the same deterministic path. 151 152 ## 📞 The calling side 153 154 The API calls through a thin client: `spawn(html, recipe or none, job id, domain)` at the source step, and `resolve(job id)` on poll. The pipeline maps the states to outcomes and writes the `extraction:`-prefixed errors; the client translates nothing. The item's extraction handle is the job id, stable across retries. A retried item re-attaches to the same running job, and the API mints a new id only when the previous job ended `error`, because that is the one terminal whose instance would hand back the same failure. The item stores the extraction domain beside the handle, because a redirect can leave the item's URL pointing somewhere other than the final host, and the recipe insert at resolve time needs the true domain. 155 156 Fetching stays API-side and always uses firecrawl. The queued ceiling measures 300 seconds from `queued_at` and fires during holds too; each accepted retry restarts the clock. A `not_article` verdict fails the item permanently, and the retry route accepts the item under its cap, the verdict included. 157 158 > [!NOTE] The ceiling can kill an item mid-authoring 159 > An authoring that outlasts about four windows exhausts the retry cap, the item dies, and its job completes unread. The recipe the job authored is lost, and the domain's next article authors fresh. Accepted knowingly. Authoring inside one window is the expected case, the turn bound is a ceiling rather than a forecast, and the ceiling's simplicity is worth more than a paused clock. 160 161 ## ⚙️ Platform limits 162 163 A workflow instance has no wall-clock limit; the bound is CPU per invocation, tens of seconds by default and configurable upward. The agent loops never approach that bound, because model turns are input-output waits. Instance parameters, step results and the returned output are each capped near 1 MiB: an article whose fetched HTML exceeds the cap fails as too large before any step runs. Finished outputs persist for the retention window, days on the free tier and a month on the paid tier, which is far longer than the poll's resolve cadence. Instance state is kept for that window too, so a job id is not reusable until the window passes. 164 165 ## ℹ️ Sources 166 167 - Cloudflare Workflows, Workers API and limits: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/workers-api/ and https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/reference/limits/ 168 - Triggering workflows, including from a Durable Object: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/trigger-workflows/ 169 - Flue on Cloudflare, agents as Durable Objects: https://flueframework.com/docs/ecosystem/deploy/cloudflare/ 170 - Flue workflows, dispatch and read from a step: https://flueframework.com/docs/guide/workflows/ 171 - The Cloudflare announcement of the Agents SDK and Flue: https://blog.cloudflare.com/agents-platform-flue-sdk/ 172 - Dynamic Workers, the open-beta primitive for runtime-given code: https://developers.cloudflare.com/dynamic-workers/ 173 174 --- 175 176 Related: [recipes](recipes.md) · [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) · [tts-service](tts-service.md) · [article-extraction](article-extraction.md) · [deployment-and-ci](deployment-and-ci.md) 177

1 --- 2 title: "Article extraction" 3 summary: "How the API fetches an article and turns the extraction service's markdown units into the item's typed units: a spoken form derived from each unit's display, a drop for a unit with nothing to say, and the acquisition of the article's declared images." 4 created: "2026-07-29" 5 --- 6 7 # Article extraction 8 9 ## 🔭 Overview 10 11 The API fetches an article's HTML, hands it to the [extraction-service](extraction-service.md), and turns what comes back into the list of typed units that every later pipeline step reads. The service runs the domain's [recipe](recipes.md) and returns a title and markdown units: paragraphs, code blocks and declared images. When the job resolves, the API derives each text unit's spoken form from its display markdown, drops a unit whose spoken form has nothing to say, and acquires each declared image. The result is one list in which every unit carries its `display`, its `type` and its `spoken` form (see [item-contract](item-contract.md)); what a described unit says comes from [the-describer](the-describer.md). 12 13 ## 🌐 Fetching the page 14 15 The fetch is a firecrawl scrape. Its raw HTML goes to the extraction service unsegmented. The domain of the final URL, after redirects, picks the recipe. A scrape that cannot reach firecrawl, or returns no HTML, fails the item with a `fetch:` reason. The API writes what each scrape bills to the cost ledger in its own commit (see [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md)), so a failed item still records the credit it spent. 16 17 The fetch sits behind a `Fetcher` interface with one implementation, so a second fetch strategy is another implementation rather than a branch inside the step. 18 19 > [!NOTE] What firecrawl is called with, and why rawHtml 20 > The scrape asks for `rawHtml` and `markdown` at `proxy="auto"`. The API asks for `rawHtml` rather than firecrawl's cleaned HTML because the cleaning throws away images (9 against 5 on one corpus article), and the recipe declares the article's images from the page's own markup. `markdown` costs no extra credit, so the API requests it as evidence; nothing reads it. `proxy="auto"` bills 1 credit when a basic proxy suffices and 5 on a stealth escalation. 21 22 > [!WARNING] firecrawl's output is non-deterministic 23 > The same URL scraped minutes apart returned a 5x spread in size, and `rawHtml` is post-JavaScript, so it can carry hydrated page chrome a plain fetch never had. The recipe's container and ignores are what keep that chrome out of the units. The spread affects re-recording a test cassette, never a replay, which returns recorded bytes verbatim. 24 25 ## 📩 How a completed job becomes typed units 26 27 ```mermaid 28 flowchart TD 29 start(["Poll: job resolves
complete, with title
and display units"]) --> loop 30 subgraph loop ["For each job unit,
in document order"] 31 direction TB 32 kind{"Image unit?"} 33 kind -->|No| spoken["1 Derive the spoken
form from the display"] 34 spoken --> test{"2 Drop rule
matches?"} 35 test -->|Yes| drop["3 Drop: no typed unit"] 36 test -->|No| keep["4 Keep as a typed
paragraph or code unit"] 37 kind -->|Yes| stash["5 Hold it after the
last kept text unit"] 38 end 39 loop --> acquire["6 Acquire held images,
interleave with kept units"] 40 acquire --> any{"7 Any unit survives?"} 41 any -. no .-> fail(["Fail: extraction:
no surviving units"]) 42 any -->|Yes| write["8 Write title, units
and recipe insert"] 43 write --> next(["Describe, synthesis,
store: survivors only"]) 44 ``` 45 46 The extraction step runs this once, on the poll that resolves a `complete` job. Steps 1 and 2 are in a required order, because the drop rule reads the spoken form. The loop must also run in document order, because step 5 anchors an image to the last text unit kept so far. When that unit is dropped, the image anchors to the kept unit before it. An image that comes before every text unit goes first in the list. Step 6 acquires the held images and drops any that will not acquire (see below). Step 7 fails the item when nothing survives, before anything is written. Step 8 writes the survivors with the title and, when the job authored or revised the recipe, the insert of its next version (see [recipes](recipes.md)). 47 48 From step 8 on, describe, synthesis and store work on the survivors only and never drop a unit, so the length guard at store compares one list against its own timeline (invariant 2). 49 50 > [!NOTE] Why the display list is persisted rather than re-extracted 51 > The display list is written onto the item when the job resolves and joined onto the timing at finalize (see [item-contract](item-contract.md)) rather than re-fetched and re-extracted when synthesis completes. Re-extracting risks a different result across the async gap: the same URL a minute later is not guaranteed to produce the same page. 52 53 ## 🗣️ Deriving the spoken form 54 55 The spoken form is derived from the unit's display markdown by walking its CommonMark token tree, so the display and spoken forms come from one extraction (invariant 1). A fenced code block becomes the fixed placeholder `"Code sample."`. A table is linearized into header-aware prose (`"Feature: Extraction, Status: done."`) rather than speaking pipe characters. Everything else keeps its `text` and inline code content, dropping heading and list markers, emphasis markers and link destinations. 56 57 A shared tail, `sanitize_spoken`, then turns any leftover emphasis or code marker into a space, drops the space a marker left before punctuation, collapses whitespace, and reduces an XML-like tagged word to the words inside it (`` to "software", `` to "div"). It accepts the escaped form of a tag as well, because the table linearizer reads a cell off the raw inline source, where the backslash still sits in front of the tag. The describer's model output runs through the same tail (see [the-describer](the-describer.md)), since a JSON schema cannot forbid a marker inside its string value. 58 59 The `"Code sample."` placeholder is the **interim** spoken form of a code block. During enrichment the describer overwrites a code unit's spoken form with `Code: ` and a describable image's with `Image: `; a code block keeps the floor `"Code with no description."` only when the describer fails or the per-item budget is spent. 60 61 > [!NOTE] The words inside a surviving tag are the article's own 62 > An author writing about software writes ``, `` or `` as text, and a tag still present in a unit's markdown is prose the author escaped. Dropping it silently loses a word the article meant to say, and a whitelist of real HTML element names would be actively wrong here, since an author writing about `
` intends the listener to hear "div". 63 64 ## 🗑️ Dropping a unit with nothing to say 65 66 ```mermaid 67 flowchart TD 68 A["Text unit from the job,
with its spoken form"] --> C{"Spoken form has a
letter or digit?"} 69 C -->|No| D((Drop)) 70 C -->|Yes| K((Keep)) 71 ``` 72 73 The rule runs on every paragraph and code unit of a completed job and reads only the spoken form: a letter inside a link URL or a code block's language tag never keeps a unit. "Letter or digit" follows Unicode, so non-Latin text is kept. An empty spoken form fails the same test. A dropped unit never becomes a typed unit, so its display, its spoken form and its timing window leave together (invariant 2), and it leaves no trace: no degradation, no log. 74 75 What the rule catches is a section-break ornament (`❦`, `* * *`, `§`) or bare punctuation that a recipe emitted as its own paragraph. A code unit always passes, because its spoken form is the `"Code sample."` placeholder. 76 77 > [!NOTE] Why a drop leaves no trace 78 > The rule drops only units whose spoken form carries no letter or digit, so what disappears is never a word the author wrote. A degradation records content the item lost, and an ornament carries no content. 79 80 > [!WARNING] A unit with nothing to pronounce crashes synthesis 81 > The synthesizer produces no audio for a paragraph made only of a symbol, and the TTS service fails the whole call on it. A sockpuppet.org recipe that kept its `❦` section breaks as paragraphs failed its items with a `tts:` error while every extraction step reported success. The drop is what keeps such a unit from reaching synthesis. 82 83 > [!TIP] Rejected: echoed-title and navigation-label matching on job units 84 > The recipe already names the title element and carries the ignore list the author agent wrote, so an echoed title or a "Contents" label is the recipe's to exclude. Matching them again in the API would add a heuristic that repeats a decision the recipe already makes. 85 86 ## 🖼️ Article images: acquisition and spoken form 87 88 The recipe declares which images belong to the article: each image unit carries its `src` and `alt`, and the API acquires exactly the images the recipe declares, with no selection of its own. Each acquired image gets a spoken form and goes after the text unit it followed in the page. Each image is an `ImageUnit` with its own spoken form and therefore its own timing window. 89 90 ### ⬇️ Acquisition: download, validate, rasterise, store 91 92 A declared image is downloaded under a per-host semaphore (default 2) beneath a global one (default 10), with a 10-second timeout and a 10 MB streamed size cap. The per-host bound is the one that matters: one article's many same-host images must never open that many connections to a server nagara has no relationship with. 93 94 Validation runs on the **decoded bytes**, never on HTTP or HTML metadata. The bytes are sniffed for an `= 200`**, measured on the decoded file. What survives is re-encoded to WebP keyed by its content hash (see [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md) for the storage seam this shares) and the hash becomes the unit's image reference, so no origin URL leaks into persisted markdown. 95 96 > [!NOTE] Why validate by decoding, not by trusting the attributes or the Content-Type 97 > Most of the corpus omits `width`/`height` entirely (all four New Yorker contact sheets carry neither), and a Content-Type header can lie, so the only trustworthy size and format come from decoding the file itself. The 200 px floor sits in a gap in the corpus: avatars and tracking pixels cluster around 40 px and every legitimate figure is 305 px or larger. Two square brand logos survive it, accepted rather than chased, because a square-ratio rule has no legitimate square image in the corpus to test against and a false positive costs only one cheap describe call. 98 99 An SVG has no pixel size to measure, so it is rasterised to PNG at a fixed 768 px width on the way in and then flows through the same pipeline as any raster image, describable and displayable. The 200 px filter does not apply to it, because the rasteriser sets its resolution. 100 101 > [!WARNING] The SVG rasteriser needs a system library Railway's image does not carry by default 102 > `cairosvg` needs the `cairo` system library, absent from Railway's build image. It is installed by a dashboard-only service variable, `RAILPACK_DEPLOY_APT_PACKAGES=libcairo2`, required and not in `railway.toml` (the same class as the Root Directory / Watch Paths settings in [deployment-and-ci](deployment-and-ci.md)). Without it, the import guard catches the `OSError` a missing system library raises (not `ImportError`) and every SVG degrades to a dropped unit rather than crashing the process. 103 104 ### 💬 An image's spoken form 105 106 An acquired image speaks its alt verbatim as `Image: `, or the floor `"Image with no description."` when the alt is empty. The good-alt filter decides whether the describer replaces that form with a generated sentence (see the precedence in [the-describer](the-describer.md)). One of its checks is the cruft test: an alt that repeats the article title, or carries no letter or digit, is not a good alt. 107 108 ### ❌ An image that will not acquire is dropped from both lists 109 110 An image that 404s, times out, exceeds the size cap, will not decode, or fails SVG rasterisation is dropped from `display` and `spoken` alike (invariant 2), and the drop is recorded as a `degradation`: a typed object `{"type": "image", "url": , "reason": }` that never rides on the wire. This is acquisition failure only, kept distinct from a **describe** failure, which never goes silent (see [the-describer](the-describer.md)). The two divide by layer: an image that never arrived has no unit to speak for, so it drops; an image that arrived but could not be described keeps a spoken fallback. 111 112 > [!NOTE] Why a degradation column, when the item is still `ready` 113 > `error` stays failed-only, and that rule is worth keeping. A `ready` item that silently dropped six of twelve images exposes nothing to the client and a full record to the operator: technically `ready` and quietly worse. The degradation list is what makes that visible without failing the item. Its scope is runtime degradations only. 114 115 ## ⏩ What is not built yet 116 117 - **Prose-boilerplate stripping.** Footer donation asides and sponsor mentions arrive as full sentences and reach the audio unless the recipe ignores them. The API does not filter them, because a generic filter risks trimming real content. 118 - **Quote voice switching**, and the blockquote and linearized-table end-to-end audio round-trip: a listener hears both in the one narrator voice, and that path is not yet validated end to end. 119 - **Comparison operators read as silence.** A bare `<` or `>` in prose (`3 < 4 and 5 > 2`) is left in both forms exactly as the author wrote it, and Kokoro voices neither character, so a listener hears "three, four". Speaking an operator as a word is a reading rule of its own and no construct in the corpus needs it yet. 120 121 --- 122 123 Related: [recipes](recipes.md) · [extraction-service](extraction-service.md) · [the-describer](the-describer.md) · [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) · [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md) · [item-contract](item-contract.md) · [tts-service](tts-service.md) · [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md) · [invariants](invariants.md) · [what-gets-read-aloud](../product-design/what-gets-read-aloud.md) 124

7	# TTS service
8	
9	## 🔭 Overview
10	
11	Renders an item's spoken paragraphs to audio on a GPU host and produces their read-along timing. Lives at `tts/app.py`, deployed as its own Modal app (`nagara-tts`), and is invoked by the API remotely rather than imported.
12	
13	> [!NOTE] The TTS code is an image definition, not a callable library
14	> The synthesis code *is* the specification of the container image that runs on the GPU host: it declares its own base image, system packages, and model bake step, and is uploaded as a unit. It cannot execute inside the API process; the API can only invoke it as a separately deployed service.
15	
16	## ♠️ What it exposes
17	
18	One remote method, `synthesize(paragraphs, voice)`, called through Modal rather than imported:
19	
20	| Member | Answers |
21	|---|---|
22	| `paragraphs: list[str]` | what to render: already the derived spoken form, one string per read-along unit |
23	| `voice: str` | which Kokoro voice to render with, defaulting to `af_heart` |
24	| → `audio_base64` | the rendered audio, base64-encoded so it survives the JSON round trip |
25	| → `format` | which codec the caller must treat it as: `audio/ogg`, or `audio/wav` on the ffmpeg fallback |
26	| → `duration` | the total audio length in seconds, what a progress bar divides by |
27	| → `paragraphs` | the position-keyed timeline, `{index, start, end}` per unit; see [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md) |
28	
29	The API's [item-contract](item-contract.md) models the return shape as `SynthesisResult`.
30	
31	## 📩 Flow
32	
33	```mermaid
34	flowchart LR
35	    P["paragraphs[]"] --> S["synthesize each paragraph with Kokoro"]
36	    S --> A["concatenate audio + 0.1s gaps"]
37	    S --> T["build_timeline: pause-fold windows"]
38	    A --> E["encode: Opus, WAV fallback"]
39	    E --> R["return audio_base64 + timeline + duration"]
40	    T --> R
41	```
42	
43	Each paragraph is synthesized independently through Kokoro-82M and its duration recorded, then the audios are concatenated with a fixed 0.1-second silence gap between them: none after the last paragraph, since there is nothing left to separate it from. [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md)'s `build_timeline` turns those per-paragraph durations into contiguous windows over the same concatenated audio. The whole result is base64-encoded and returned as one payload, with the timeline's `text` set to the paragraph actually synthesized; the API replaces it with the display markdown at the join described in [article-extraction](article-extraction.md), never this value.
44	
45	Audio is encoded to Opus through a `soundfile`-then-`ffmpeg` pipeline; if that codec path fails, it falls back to plain WAV. "Playable audio" is the only property either path is judged on, and WAV runs roughly 18 times larger than the equivalent Opus for a full article.
46	
47	GPU and memory snapshotting are both enabled on the deployed class, bringing cold start down from roughly 27 seconds to roughly 6; a container then stays warm for 300 seconds after its last call, to absorb a session's burst of pushes.
48	
49	## 📡 How the API invokes it with no broker
50	
51	The API **spawns** a remote call through Modal's class handle (`modal.Cls.from_name(app, cls)().synthesize.spawn(paragraphs, voice)`) and persists the returned call's `object_id` on the item as the handle to resolve later (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)); the enqueue request then returns immediately.
52	
53	The result is resolved **lazily**, on each poll, with a non-blocking read whose exception type is what tells a running job from a crashed one: a `TimeoutError` means still running, and any other exception is the crash, whose message becomes the item's error.
54	
55	```python
56	result = fc.get(timeout=0)  # TimeoutError while running; any other exception is the crash
57	```
58	
59	A crashed call re-raises the remote exception across the process boundary.
60	
61	> [!NOTE] Why the compute platform is the async layer, and there is no broker
62	> The platform's own invocation primitives (spawn plus a non-blocking result read) are sufficient async infrastructure at this scale: the running-versus-crashed distinction comes for free from the result read, not from anything the API tracks separately. The two deployables also ship independently: the TTS service ships on its own deploy cadence (see [deployment-and-ci](deployment-and-ci.md)), decoupled from the API.
63	
64	> [!TIP] Rejected: a broker and a worker process
65	> A conventional task-queue stack, a message broker plus a separate worker, would add infrastructure to run, scale, and monitor for no benefit the platform's own spawn/poll primitives do not already provide, and it would still need the same crash/running bookkeeping the result read gives for free.
66	
67	> [!NOTE] Clients poll; the API never pushes completion
68	> A client observes `generating` until a poll transitions the item to `ready` or `failed`. There is no notification path; see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) for the state machine this participates in.
69	
70	The execution layer is coupled to Modal as a result: moving off it means replacing both the compute host and the async layer, and the GPU with them.
71	
72	## ⏩ What is not built yet
73	
74	Streaming paragraph audio from one warm container, so time-to-first-audio is roughly one to two seconds instead of waiting for the whole article. Word-level timestamps exist inside Kokoro but are not returned or used; a caption export would be the consumer that asks for them.
75

7	# Item contract
8	
9	
10	## 🔭 Overview
11	
12	The HTTP routes and JSON a client (Tachikoma today; the read-along player, not yet built in `web/`, later) reads and writes. The item routes all sit behind the auth guard ([authentication](authentication.md)), plus one public liveness route.
13	
14	
15	## ♠️ What it exposes
16	
17	An `ItemResponse`, its `units` list carrying one `UnitResponse` per read-along window once timed:
18	
19	| Field | Answers |
20	|---|---|
21	| `id`, `url`, `title` | which item this is, and the article it points at |
22	| `status` | `queued`, `generating`, `ready`, or `failed`: the state machine in [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) |
23	| `voice` | which Kokoro voice this item's audio uses, fixed at creation |
24	| `created_at` | when it was enqueued |
25	| `duration` | total audio length once `ready`; absent until then |
26	| `units[]` | the read-along list, one element per display unit; `null` until every window is timed, see below |
27	| `error` | populated only when `status` is `failed` |
28	| `audio_url` (computed, not stored) | present only once `ready`, so a client never has to check status before deciding whether to trust the link |
29	
30	A display unit is a pydantic discriminated union on `type`, one of `paragraph`, `code`, or `image`. Each variant carries its rendered markdown in `display`, its `type`, and an internal `spoken` form; an image unit adds `image`, a content hash. The persisted unit holds all of that; the wire element drops `spoken` and adds the timing window:
31	
32	| Shape | Carries |
33	|---|---|
34	| persisted `Unit` | `type`, `display`, `spoken`, plus `image` on an image unit |
35	| wire `UnitResponse` | `index`, `type`, `display`, `start`, `end`, plus `image` on an image unit |
36	
37	`units` is `null` until every window is timed, and carries the complete timed list from `ready` onward.
38	
39	> [!NOTE] The spoken form never reaches a client
40	> `display` and `spoken` come from one markdown segmentation on one unit; the spoken form is a synthesis detail, joined onto the timing at finalize and then filtered out by the response model rather than exposed (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)). Projecting it out at the response boundary is the mechanism behind invariant 1's oldest clause: no client ever reads the spoken text, and the display form is never synthesized. A caption-export route that needs the spoken form gets its own field then; no consumer needs it today.
41	
42	> [!NOTE] Why the list is held back until it is timed
43	> A wire element carries `start` and `end`, and timing only exists once synthesis finishes. Poll persists the units when the extraction job resolves, with `type`/`display`/`spoken` but no window, and enrichment rewrites them, so a partial, untimed list sits on the row while the item is `queued` or `generating`. Returning `null` until the list is timed keeps that partial state off the wire, so a client never renders half an article. Nothing is lost: a client polling a not-yet-`ready` item has no timeline to render against anyway.
44	
45	## 🛣️ What each route does
46	
47	| Route | Does |
48	|---|---|
49	| `POST /items` | Create an item from `{url, voice?}`. Returns `202` with the item at `queued`; a background task then fetches the article and spawns its extraction job, and poll drives the rest (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)). |
50	| `GET /items/{id}` | Poll. Advances a `generating` item: resolves its extraction job, describes its images and code, then spawns and resolves synthesis. Fails a `queued` item, or a `generating` item still waiting on its extraction job, once its work age has passed the ceiling. Then returns the current item. `404` for an unknown id. |
51	| `GET /items/{id}/audio` | Serve audio for a `ready` item, via [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md)'s audio store. `404` if the item is not `ready`, has no audio format yet, or is unknown: no link is ever minted for a non-ready item. |
52	| `GET /items/{id}/images/{hash}` | Serve an image for the item, keyed by the content hash carried on an image unit. Minted fresh at read time: a file locally, a short-lived presigned URL in the bucket. `404` for an unknown item. An unknown *hash* answers differently per backend, which is deliberate; see below. Behind the same key as everything else. |
53	| `POST /items/{id}/retry` | Re-drive a `failed` item in place, resuming from the phase that failed. `202` with the item back at `queued`; `409` unless the item is `failed` and under the retry cap, `404` for an unknown id. See the section below and [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md). |
54	| `GET /health` | The one unauthenticated route; carries no item data. |
55	
56	Voice selection: an enqueue request that names a voice uses it; one that omits it gets a voice chosen at random from a curated pool at creation time (`pick_voice()`, `VOICE_POOL` in `api/app/service/tts.py`), recorded on the item, and stable across every later poll.
57	
58	The `url` string reaches the pipeline as given: nothing at the route or the schema validates it, and the first thing that can refuse it is the fetch itself, which fails the item with `fetch: no response` when the fetcher returns nothing at all.
59	
60	## 🖼️ Image serving
61	
62	`GET /items/{id}/images/{hash}` serves an image that belongs to the article. An image unit carries the content hash in its `image` field; a client reconstructs the path from the item id and the hash. The route requires the key, so invariant 4 holds uniformly.
63	
64	> [!NOTE] The URL is minted at read time, never persisted
65	> A presigned URL written into the row would be dead inside `s3_url_ttl` (3600s), and the unit list is persisted indefinitely. The store serves a `FileResponse` locally and a fresh presigned redirect in the bucket, reconstructing the object from the hash each request. The image object is keyed by a content hash of its re-encoded WebP bytes, not the item id or the origin URL, so one image is stored once and dedupes across items and re-enqueues.
66	
67	An unknown hash is the one place the two backends do not answer alike. Locally the store stats the file and raises the API's own `404`. In the bucket it mints the presigned URL without asking whether the object is there, so the client gets a `307` to a real signed URL that then answers `404` in the store's own format.
68	
69	> [!NOTE] Why the backends are allowed to disagree here
70	> Matching them means a `HEAD` per request, and this route is hot in a way the audio one is not: audio is one file per item fetched once, images are many per item fetched on every render. A round-trip per image to convert a store `404` into an API `404` is a poor trade when both already say not-found.
71	>
72	> The audio route has the same shape and does not have the same exposure, because it gates on `ready` and a recorded audio format first, so a missing object there is a genuine anomaly rather than a routine miss. Image serving has no equivalent gate on purpose, per the association warning below.
73	>
74	> A caller that needs one uniform shape should treat any non-`200` from this route as absent rather than reading the body.
75	
76	> [!WARNING] The item lookup checks existence, not association
77	> The route 404s an unknown item id but never checks that the hash belongs to that item, because the object is keyed by content hash alone so one image stores once and dedupes across items. Under today's single shared key that is not an escalation: there is nothing to reach that the key does not already grant. Per-key quota and API-key management are not built yet; once they are, the item id in the path is decoration and one key can read another key's images by hash, so whoever builds per-key auth must either check the hash against the item's own units or accept that images are shared across keys.
78	
79	## 🔁 Retry
80	
81	`POST /items/{id}/retry` re-drives a failed item in place rather than re-enqueuing the URL. It refuses anything but a `failed` item, and a `failed` item past the retry cap, with `409`; `404` for an unknown id. An accepted retry sets the item back to `queued`, rewrites `queued_at`, advances `retry_count`, clears the old error, and hands the item to the queued lifecycle task, the same task enqueue uses.
82	
83	What the task does depends on how far the previous run got: [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) carries each case and what it costs.
84	
85	> [!NOTE] Double-submitting is refused by the write, not by the read
86	> The transition is one conditional `UPDATE` gating on status still `failed` and `retry_count` under the cap, incrementing the count in SQL. A rowcount of zero is the `409`. Reading the row first and then writing would let two concurrent retries both pass the guard, which costs two Modal spawns for one item and increments the count once, so the cap would read tighter than it is. The pre-read only picks which refusal message to send.
87	
88	> [!NOTE] Why the cap is local and quota is not
89	> The per-item retry cap (`retry_max`, default 3) is a cheap local bound on the worst case: a flapping item spends at most a few synthesises before it stays failed. Broader per-key and quota enforcement is deliberately not built here. The cap does not need the full hardening apparatus, and building half of one here would be worse than either.
90	
91	## ⏩ What is not built yet
92	
93	- **Quota and API-key management.** No enforcement and no create/revoke route exist yet.
94	- **A list endpoint.** There is no `GET /items` today; a client tracks ids itself.
95	- **Word-level timing.** One window per unit, not per word, by design; see [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md).

6	
7	# The describer
8	
9	
10	## 🔭 Overview
11	
12	Gives a listener one spoken sentence for a block they cannot see: a code block, or an image with no author-written text. It is a reusable core with two callers: the code path and the image path both reach the same Gemini call, layered under a fan-out that floors, caps, and fails per unit. It never speaks what a block *means*, only what it *is* or *shows*: meaning comes from the author, and the describer only makes the block visible. Implemented in `api/app/service/describe.py`, called during enrichment (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)).
13	
14	
15	> [!NOTE] The describer is unchanged by the recipes architecture
16	> Recipes stop at units ([recipes](recipes.md)); describing code and images stays this generic path, whatever extracted them.
17	
18	## ♠️ What it exposes
19	
20	| Member | Answers |
21	|---|---|
22	| `describe(client, contents)` | the reusable core: one structured-output call plus the sanitize tail, returning the spoken sentence. The caller owns `contents`: a prompt string, or a prompt plus an inline image part |
23	| `build_code_prompt(title, intro, code)` | the code prompt: kind and what-for, no opener, the introducing unit as authority |
24	| `build_image_prompt(title, alt)` | the image prompt: one specific sentence of what is shown, alt passed as unreliable context |
25	| `ImageDescribeRequest` | one image the precedence flagged for a describe (case 2): its `index` in the unit list, its raw `alt`, and the WebP `image` bytes |
26	| `enrich_with_descriptions(...)` | the fan-out: describe every code unit and every flagged image against one shared budget, in document order, returning the updated units and a degradation list |
27	
28	## 📞 The core call: structured output, then sanitize
29	
30	`describe` makes one call to `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` on Google's paid API (never through a gateway), parses the JSON, and runs the value through the shared sanitize tail. The response schema is a JSON object with one required string field, `spoken`.
31	
32	The response is requested as `application/json` against that schema, so the model returns `{"spoken": "..."}` and there is nothing to parse out of prose. The parsed `spoken` then passes through `sanitize_spoken`, the same tail article prose runs through (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)).
33	
34	> [!NOTE] Both guards, because a leaked marker is stochastic and only ever caught by ear
35	> Structured output makes one whole failure class impossible: the model cannot open with a heading or a preamble when the value is a bare string field. But a JSON schema cannot forbid a backtick or a `**` *inside* that string, and a marker reached narration exactly once in the bake-off and did not reproduce across 48 re-runs. "It did not happen this time" is the judgement a pipeline cannot rely on, so sanitize catches the marker the schema cannot.
36	
37	> [!NOTE] The schema is not repeated in the prompt
38	> Gemini's own docs warn that duplicating the schema, or JSON examples, in the prompt lowers output quality. The config carries the shape; the prompt describes only the task.
39	
40	## ✍️ The prompts: no opener, an invention guard, minimal asymmetric context
41	
42	Both prompts share three rules and differ only in subject.
43	
44	**No self-opener.** The sentence must begin with the thing itself, the kind-noun for code or the visible subject for an image, and the word "This" is forbidden anywhere in it. `Code: ` and `Image: ` are nagara's announcement, so the model owns only the content. An image noun-opens naturally; code needs the ban spelled out, because forbidding "This block" and "This example" alone leaves a residual "This is a…".
45	
46	**The invention guard** is a sharpened positive instruction with no few-shot. Code: name the kind and the purpose, never the mechanics, return values, or framework, unless the introducing text states them. Image: describe only what is visibly there, and **name no person, organization, brand, place, or region unless that exact name appears as written text inside the image**. The one confirmed invention in the bake-off was geography read onto an artwork, and no run under this guard reproduced it.
47	
48	**Context is minimal and asymmetric.** The code prompt gets the article title, the introducing paragraph (the unit just before, which the listener heard seconds ago as authority), and the block. The paragraph *after* is dropped. The image prompt gets the title and the alt, labelled as often wrong or SEO filler, to use only where it matches the pixels.
49	
50	> [!NOTE] Why the paragraph after the block is dropped
51	> It is the elaboration the listener is about to hear anyway, and including it nudges the model toward describing behaviour rather than naming what the block is.
52	
53	> [!NOTE] Why one sentence per code block, even when the prose already named it
54	> Every code block gets its own spoken sentence because it needs its own audio window in the read-along, and dropping it would remove the code from a reader's view. The redundancy with the introducing prose is the price of that window. What the sentence adds above restatement is the *kind*: "the syntax for creating a variable" names the concept; the specific field names and query values that would add most are exactly what the guard forbids as invention.
55	
56	## 🗣️ What each unit says
57	
58	A **code** unit's spoken form becomes `Code: <sentence>`, overwriting the interim `"Code sample."` placeholder from the spoken-form derivation.
59	
60	An **image** follows a four-step precedence, top to bottom. Cases 1, 3, and 4 are the fallback already on the unit from acquisition (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)); the describer owns case 2 and the filter that routes between 1 and 2.
61	
62	| # | Condition | Spoken form |
63	|---|---|---|
64	| 1 | good alt | the alt, verbatim |
65	| 2 | no good alt | **one generated sentence of what the image shows** |
66	| 3 | generation failed, alt non-empty | any alt, verbatim |
67	| 4 | generation failed, alt empty | `Image with no description.` |
68	
69	The **good-alt filter** (`_is_good_alt`) decides case 1 against case 2. Alt is trusted verbatim only when it reads as a grammatical sentence, is not the article title (the cruft test in [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)), and clears a small CMS denylist (`subscribe`, `appears in`, `courtesy`, `photograph by`, `click`) and filename patterns. Everything else goes to the describer: empty, keyword soup, title-as-alt, a subscribe prompt.
70	
71	> [!NOTE] The denylist separates good alt from boilerplate where no clean heuristic exists
72	> "Image of tank rolling over a world map" and "This article appears in the October 2023 issue. Subscribe to WIRED." are *both* grammatical sentences, so grammaticality alone cannot separate good alt from boilerplate. The denylist keeps the first and sends the second to the describer, at the cost of a maintained list a novel boilerplate phrase can slip past.
73	
74	> [!NOTE] A describe failure never goes silent
75	> On failure or over-budget, an image keeps its precedence fallback (any non-empty alt, else the floor), so invariant 2's drop-from-both never fires for a *description* failure. It fires one layer earlier, for an *acquisition* failure, which belongs to [article-extraction](article-extraction.md). The floor is honest: it tells the listener an image is there that could not be described.
76	
77	## 🔀 The fan-out, and its bounds
78	
79	`enrich_with_descriptions` walks the interleaved unit list once into one document-ordered job list of every code unit and every flagged image. That single ordered list is what makes the cap a shared budget across both kinds.
80	
81	```mermaid
82	flowchart TD
83	    J["jobs in document order: code units + flagged images"] --> C{"within the per-item cap?"}
84	    C -->|beyond cap| Floor["code floors; image keeps its precedence fallback; degrade: cap reached"]
85	    C -->|within cap| G["asyncio.gather(return_exceptions=True), under a semaphore"]
86	    G --> R{"per job"}
87	    R -->|success| W["overwrite spoken with Code:/Image: sentence; meter one billed call"]
88	    R -->|failure| D["code floors; image keeps fallback; degrade: describe failed"]
89	    W --> S{"code units within cap and none resolved?"}
90	    D --> S
91	    S -->|yes| Fail["raise: every code unit failed is an outage"]
92	    S -->|no| Done["return units + degradations"]
93	```
94	
95	**One shared budget, counted in document order.** `NAGARA_DESCRIBE_MAX_PER_ITEM` (default 25) caps the combined code-and-image total, so the two kinds can never each spend a full budget. Past the cap a code unit floors and an image keeps its precedence fallback; each records a `describe cap reached` degradation. The cap never fails an item and never goes silent.
96	
97	**Independent resolution.** `asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True)` under an `asyncio.Semaphore` (`NAGARA_DESCRIBE_CONCURRENCY`, default 10) lets every job resolve on its own, so a fifty-unit article where one call fails keeps the other forty-nine.
98	
99	> [!NOTE] Why every job resolves independently
100	> Enrichment commits the whole unit list in one step, so one failed call must not discard the others: each job resolves on its own, a failure floors or falls back that unit alone, and the step's write carries the mixed result. Independent resolution is the only shape that keeps a single bad call at the unit level rather than the item's.
101	
102	**Retry policy.** google-genai does not retry on its own, so `stamina` owns it: roughly three attempts with exponential backoff and jitter, classified by which errors are worth retrying.
103	
104	```python
105	_RETRY_STATUS = frozenset({408, 429})  # + any 5xx, + connection/timeout
106	```
107	
108	408, 429, and 5xx mean unlucky or briefly down and retry in place; 400, 401, 403, and 404 mean the call itself is wrong and fail the unit at once, because retrying only burns the budget.
109	
110	**Per-unit failure degrades, systemic failure fails the item.** A single unit failing writes a `describe failed` degradation and floors (code) or keeps the fallback (image). The item fails only when there are code units within the cap and **every one** of them failed: a code-bearing item with zero code descriptions is a silent total failure, an outage rather than an article state. An image-only failure never raises, because an image always has a spoken fallback.
111	
112	> [!WARNING] The client is never built from an empty key
113	> A missing `NAGARA_GEMINI_API_KEY` raises rather than letting google-genai fall back to the ambient `GOOGLE_API_KEY`/`GEMINI_API_KEY` it reads on its own: a trap that succeeds silently on a developer's machine and fails in production. The key has to be set in the Railway dashboard, because `railway.toml` carries no environment variables.
114	
115	Each successful call fires an `on_describe(kind)` callback, which the lifecycle meters as one `describer` cost entry per call; a failed or capped unit made no billable call, so only the success branch counts.
116	
117	## ⏩ What is not built yet
118	
119	- **No describer cache.** Per-row resume already covers the common retry case. What is lost is cross-article dedup of the same snippet, second-order on cost; a cache does not defend against abuse, and the retry count cap and quota enforcement, which is not built yet, own that instead.
120	- **The fallback model is not wired.** `gemini-3.1-flash-lite` is named in the code as the fallback for when 3.5 is unavailable, but nothing ever selects it: every call goes to `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`, and `stamina` retry covers transient unavailability. It stays unwired because under structured output it was seen to write "A TypeScript interface…" for a one-line JSON block, a kind-level error rather than a behaviour-level one.
121

6	
7	# What gets read aloud
8	
9	## 🔭 Overview
10	
11	What a listener hears, independent of the markdown mechanism in [article-extraction](../technical-design/article-extraction.md) that produces it.
12	
13	## 📰 Only the article body
14	
15	A listener never hears a navigation label or the article's own title read as part of the article, and a paragraph with no real words, such as a section-break ornament, is silently dropped before synthesis. Some boilerplate still gets through: a footer donation ask or a sponsor mention arrives as ordinary prose sentences and nothing yet tells it apart from real content.
16	
17	Footnotes are left out of both the page and the audio: neither the reference markers nor the footnote text is read, so a listener hears "in a loop, at a bare minimum" rather than "in a loop one at a bare minimum".
18	
19	## 🔣 How non-prose constructs are read
20	
21	- **Emphasis, links, and headings** read as their plain words: a link says its anchor text, never the URL underneath it.
22	- **A list item** reads as its own sentence, marker dropped.
23	- **A blockquote** reads as clean prose, quote marks dropped.
24	- **A code block** is described in one spoken sentence rather than read aloud: the listener hears what kind of code it is and what it is for, announced with a spoken `Code:` cue ("Code: A Python variable definition."). The source is never read back, and the sentence never claims what the code does. When no description can be made, the listener hears a short honest line ("Code with no description.") rather than silence.
25	- **An XML-like tagged word** an author wrote about (`<software>`, `<your-api-key>`, `<T>`) reads as the words inside it, brackets dropped, so the listener hears "software" and "your API key". A reader still sees the brackets on the page, because they are the author's own notation for a placeholder or a generic.
26	- **A table** reads as header-aware prose ("Feature: Extraction, Status: done.") rather than speaking pipe characters.
27	- **An image** is described in the author's own words when there are any, and otherwise in one generated sentence of what it shows. In order of preference the listener hears: the author's alt text, when it is a real sentence; else one generated sentence of what the image shows, announced with an `Image:` cue; else any alt there is; else an honest "Image with no description." rather than silence.
28	
29	## ✍️ The author's words win, and a description only makes an image visible
30	
31	Both a code sentence and an image description are generated, so a very code- or image-heavy article carries a budget: only so many descriptions are made. The descriptions go to the blocks that come first in reading order; past the budget a code block falls to its honest short line, and an image falls down its precedence to alt or to the floor. The article still plays start to finish, never failed or silenced for being over budget.
32	
33	> [!NOTE] A description makes an image visible, it never says what it means
34	> Meaning comes only from the author, so a real alt sentence always wins where it exists. A generated sentence says what is shown, the decaying fish on the sand, the axes of a chart, and stops there: it makes the image visible without reading anything into it.
35	
36	> [!NOTE] A code sentence is generated even when the prose just introduced the block
37	> A tutorial usually names a block in the sentence right before it, so the spoken description often restates what the listener just heard. It is generated anyway: dropping it would take the code off the page for the reader too, which in a tutorial is a real loss, so the block keeps both its window in the audio and its place on the page.
38	
39	> [!NOTE] A flawed alt is spoken only when a description could not be made
40	> Alt that is a subscribe prompt, keyword soup, or a bare filename is what sends an image to a generated description in the first place, so it is never spoken on the normal path. It returns only as a last resort, when the description itself could not be produced, because a clumsy line that says an image is there still beats silence that hides it.
41	
42	> [!NOTE] The audio is clean because of what is extracted, not because of a separate reading mode
43	> The player renders the same markdown the listener never hears directly. The domain's [recipe](../technical-design/recipes.md) decides what reaches the markdown, and the spoken-form derivation in [article-extraction](../technical-design/article-extraction.md) decides how that markdown is read, so a change to what gets read aloud is a change to one of those two.
44	
45	## ⏩ What is not built yet
46	
47	A bare comparison operator is silent: `3 < 4` reads as "three, four", because the character is left as the author wrote it and the voice has no word for it. Speaking one aloud is a reading rule of its own and nothing in the corpus asks for it yet.
48	
49	Speaking a quote in a voice distinct from the narration, and adjustable playback speed, are not built.
50

3	## Question A — are sanitize_spoken steps 2-4 still needed?
4	
5	**Prod-data (describer output, code/image units): zero diffs across all 8 items.** Steps 2-4
6	on vs off produced byte-identical output for every persisted `spoken` string in
7	`reports/prod-data/itm_*.json` — describer text is plain English written by an LLM, never
8	markdown, so it carries none of `**`/`_`/`` ` ``/`~~` to begin with. Steps 2-4 are a pure
9	no-op there.
10	
11	**Round-4 units: 4 diffs out of ~50 non-list/code/image units, in `list_mode=items`.**
12	- `runin-r4` (`**review.**Agents`): ON turns the marker into the word-boundary space that
13	  makes this "review. Agents"; OFF leaves the literal asterisks glued to the next word.
14	  Audible, still needed.
15	- `tbl-3` (`**Design doc first**` table cell): same pattern — ON strips the bold marker
16	  cleanly; OFF reads the literal asterisks. Audible, still needed.
17	- `list-9` (checkbox list): ON vs OFF differ only in a doubled space after `[x]`/`[ ]` (a
18	  GFM-plugin bullet-spacing artifact). Not audible — cosmetic only.
19	- `math-2` (the display-mode formula): ON *deletes* the literal `*` in
20	  `value_0 * 2^{-days_since_decision}`, because step 2's marker-strip regex matches any bare
21	  `*` character regardless of whether markdown-it actually parsed it as emphasis. This `*`
22	  is round 4's own bare-alttext math substitution (no delimiters, per the settled rule) —
23	  it's a multiplication sign, not markdown. **Audible and wrong**: the spoken formula loses
24	  its times-operator entirely.
25	
26	**Answer: still needed, but not safe as written.** GFM markdown still produces real
27	`**`/`_`/`` ` ``/`~~` sequences that must be stripped (run-in emphasis, table cells) — turndown
28	moving off trafilatura didn't remove that need. But sanitize's step 2 is a blind regex over
29	the joined *text*, not a check on markdown-it's own token classification, so it cannot tell
30	a markdown marker from a literal character that happens to look like one. Round 4's own math
31	rule is the first case in this spike to actually put a literal `*` into spoken text, and it
32	exposes the gap immediately. A safer step 2 would strip based on the parser's own
33	emphasis/strong token boundaries rather than a raw-text regex; not attempted here since it's
34	outside this round's settled scope — noted for a future round.
35	
36	## Question B — what does the TTS do with these cases?
37	
38	Modal auth and the app lookup (`modal.Cls.from_name('nagara-tts', 'Kokoro')`) worked on the
39	first try, no blocker. All 11 cases synthesized; see `audio/manifest.json` for exact text and
40	duration per file, `audio/LISTEN.md` for what to listen for.
41	
42	**Kokoro's own default (`KPipeline.__call__`'s `split_pattern='\n+'`) already splits on
43	newlines internally**, and `tts/app.py`'s `_synth_paragraph` concatenates every resulting
44	chunk with **zero gap** — the `PAUSE_S` silence in `app.py` only sits between separate
45	entries of the `paragraphs` list argument, never between kokoro's own internal
46	newline-splits inside one paragraph string. So a round-4 newline-joined list is, in the
47	final audio, N independently-synthesized fragments glued back-to-back with no pause and no
48	shared prosody across the join — while the same list space-joined stays one single kokoro
49	call, since a bare space never matches `split_pattern`. This means the newline-vs-space
50	choice has no timing/pause consequence in the output; whatever a listener notices has to be
51	a prosody reset at each line boundary, not silence or spacing.
52	
53	Durations bear this out: newline- and space-joined pairs land within a few hundred
54	milliseconds of each other (unordered list: 18.98s vs 18.65s; ordered: 14.80s vs 14.70s) —

57	(10.78s) is 0.6s longer than `checkbox-stripped` (10.15s) — both consistent with the "off"/
58	"kept" variants literally containing more spoken material (the leftover `**` markers, the
59	literal `[x]`/`[ ]` brackets). Whether that extra material renders as garbled noise, as
60	spoken-aloud punctuation ("asterisk", "bracket x bracket"), or as something else, and whether
61	the per-line prosody resets in the newline-joined lists sound natural or choppy, is the
62	human's call — I cannot judge audio by ear. See `audio/LISTEN.md`.

64	## What round 4 changed vs round 3
65	
66	The isolated fresh author (given only the base recipe contract, the round-4 rules, and the
67	article — no inventory/findings) settled a clean recipe on its first validator run. Against
68	round 3:

--- title: "Markdown units" summary: "What a unit's display markdown carries for each source element, and how the runtime converts, validates, splits and titles it." created: "2026-09-27" --- # Markdown units ## 🔭 Overview A unit's `display` is markdown, and this note is what that markdown carries for each source element and how the runtime produces it. Every recipe hands its selected elements to one shared converter rather than converting by hand ([recipes](recipes.md)), so the mapping from source to markdown is the same across every domain. The runtime then validates the recipe's declared units, splits a list around any code block or image nested inside it, and prepends the title, in that order, before anything crosses to the API or shows up in an authoring agent's own view of what it built. ## 📄 What a unit's display carries | Source | Unit | Display markdown | |---|---|---| | A heading (`h1`–`h6`) | paragraph unit | ATX, `#` through `######` | | A blockquote | paragraph unit | `>`-prefixed; a list or table nested inside the quote stays inside the quote's own unit | | A list, ordered or unordered | one paragraph unit | `-` bullets, or ordinals that keep the source's own numbers, including a non-1 `start` | | A task-list item | inside its list's unit | `[x]` / `[ ]` | | A table | paragraph unit | a GFM pipe table | | Struck-through text | inside its unit | `~~text~~` | | A formula | inside its unit | its alttext as plain text, no delimiter | | Inline content with no GFM form | inside its unit | whatever Turndown outputs for it | | A `
` or `
` | its own code unit | a fenced code block |
| An image | its own image unit | `src` and `alt` as the page presents them, no markdown |
| A blockquote's `
`/`` | left out | — |
| A `
` | left out | — |
| Footnote references and the footnote list | left out | — |
| A heading's self-link | left out (the heading's own text stays) | — |
| The article's title | the first unit, ahead of every recipe-declared unit | `# `, from `extraction.title`; no other unit carries the title |

> [!NOTE] Why the title is synthesized, never authored
> The title unit is built from `extraction.title` after every recipe-declared unit is in hand, not selected by the recipe itself. A recipe that also selects the page's own heading as a unit still yields exactly one title, because the two are independent: the synthesized title never duplicates a recipe's heading, and a recipe never has to recognise or exclude its own page's title to avoid saying it twice.

### A worked example: a list split around a nested code block

```html
<ol>
  <li>Item A</li>
  <li>Item B
    <ol>
      <li>Item B.1</li>
      <li>Item B.2 with a code block:
        <pre><code>x = 1</code></pre>
      </li>
      <li>Item B.3</li>
    </ol>
  </li>
</ol>
```

comes back as three units, in document order:

1. a paragraph unit, the list up to the code block:
   ```
   1. Item A
   2. Item B
      1. Item B.1
      2. Item B.2 with a code block:
   ```
2. a code unit: `x = 1`
3. a paragraph unit, the list resumed:
   ```
   2.  3. Item B.3
   ```

The resumed part opens with an empty item at each enclosing level it needs to re-enter: the outer `2.` re-enters item B without repeating its text, and the inner `3.` picks the nested list back up at its own next number. It is valid CommonMark, and the same tree a listener's page renders is what the spoken-form derivation walks (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)).

## 🔄 How an element becomes markdown

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Recipe runs:<br/>declared units,<br/>display from toMarkdown"] --> V{"1 Validator:<br/>inventory, leftover,<br/>nesting, orphaned li"}
    V -->|Problems| R(("Report to the<br/>agent: revise"))
    V -->|Clean| S{"2 A list unit holding<br/>a pre or an image?"}
    S -->|Yes| P["3 Split into list part,<br/>code or image unit,<br/>list part, in order"]
    S -->|No| T
    P --> C["4 Convert each list part:<br/>own tag kept, pre gets<br/>code, Turndown + GFM"]
    C --> T["5 Prepend # title<br/>from the extracted title"]
    T --> O(("Flattened units,<br/>also what the<br/>agent sees"))
```

One converter, `toMarkdown`, serves every recipe: a recipe never converts an element by hand. It serializes the element itself, its own tag included, into Turndown with the fixed configuration (ATX headings, fenced code, `-` bullets, `---` rules) plus the GFM plugin, so the tag is what selects the markdown construct: a heading's `h2`, a quote's `blockquote`, a list's `ol` or `ul` each key a Turndown rule that only fires when that tag is present. A `<pre>` with no `<code>` child gets its content wrapped in `<code>` before conversion, so every `<pre>` becomes a fenced block regardless of how the source built it.

The same validator runs at authoring, revision and extraction, against the real element paths the recipe declared: unchanged by this ([recipes](recipes.md)). Only once validation is clean does the runtime split a list unit that holds a code block or an image, at any nesting depth, into list part, code-or-image unit, list part, in document order; a part is converted with the same `toMarkdown`, its own list tag intact. The title unit is prepended last. What the workflow returns, and what an authoring or revising agent's extract tool shows, is this same flattened list ([extraction-service](extraction-service.md)).

> [!NOTE] Why the split happens after validation, not before
> The validator's nesting check flags any two units whose paths sit inside one another, and a list-part clone produced by splitting has no path at all: it was never part of the parsed article tree, so nothing can resolve its position back into it. Validating the recipe's own declared units first, while they are still real elements at real positions, and only then splitting the already-valid result into a markdown-level list of parts, keeps every validated path real and keeps a split part from ever needing one.

> [!WARNING] The validator does not check that a unit kept its markdown
> Inventory and leftover-text checks confirm that every element in the container is accounted for and that no readable text was dropped; neither confirms that the syntax a unit was supposed to carry, a heading's `#`, a quote's `>`, a list's numbering, survived the conversion. A recipe can pass validation while a unit's display has silently lost the marker that was supposed to distinguish it from a plain paragraph.

> [!TIP] Rejected: splitting a list by handing each item to the converter on its own
> An item pulled out of its enclosing `<ol>` or `<ul>` and converted alone loses the context Turndown's list rule keys off: without a parent list tag to report a position inside, the item converts with no ordinal and no bullet, worse than the whole list would have been. The runtime instead keeps every surviving list part inside a clone of the original list's own tag, so each part still carries something to number or bullet from.

> [!TIP] Rejected: wrapping a formula's alttext in `$…$` or `$$…$$`
> The spoken-form derivation's sanitize tail knows the markdown markers Turndown can emit and turns each into silence or a word; it has no rule for a dollar sign, so a delimiter would read straight through into the audio as a literal character. The alttext carries no delimiter at all instead, and reads as plain words on both sides of the boundary.

32	## ✍️ The author's words win, and a description only makes an image visible
33

The descriptions go to the blocks that come first in reading order; past the budget a code block falls to its honest short line, and an image falls down its precedence to alt or to the floor. 36	> [!NOTE] A description makes an image visible, it never says what it means

40	> A tutorial usually names a block in the sentence right before it, so the spoken description often restates what the listener just heard. 43	> Alt that is a subscribe prompt, keyword soup, or a bare filename is what sends an image to a generated description in the first place, so it is never spoken on the normal path. 48	## ⏩ What is not built yet
49	
50	Speaking a quote in a voice distinct from the narration, and adjustable playback speed, are not built.
